Where is Cheyenne and how is the city laid out?

Cheyenne is the capital of Wyoming and the county seat of Laramie County, in the far southeast corner of the state. It sits at about 6,086 feet above sea level on Crow Creek and Dry Creek, and covers a little over 32 square miles.

Two interstates meet southwest of town. I-25 runs north to south and I-80 runs east to west, and I-180 loops through the city along US 85. Cheyenne Regional Airport offers daily nonstop United Express flights to Denver, and local buses run through the Cheyenne Transit Program. A seller here is rarely more than a few minutes from a major road, which matters when a buyer asks about commute times.

The city has several historic districts, and homes inside them may face extra review:

  • Downtown Cheyenne Historic District
  • Lakeview Historic District
  • Rainsford Historic District
  • Capitol North Historic District
  • South Side Historic District

If your house sits inside one of these areas, ask the city's Planning and Development office what applies before you spend money on repairs.

What is the short history of Cheyenne?

The Union Pacific Railroad platted Cheyenne on July 5, 1867, and the first train rolled in on November 14 of that year. The city has been Wyoming's only capital since it was named the temporary territorial capital on May 7, 1869.

Fort D. A. Russell was founded in September 1867 and later became Francis E. Warren Air Force Base in October 1949. That base is one of the oldest continuously active military installations in the country, and it still shapes the housing market through transfers and deployments.

Wyoming became a state on July 10, 1890.

What drives the Cheyenne economy?

Government, transportation, the military and a growing technology sector carry the Cheyenne economy. State offices, Union Pacific and BNSF rail yards, and F.E. Warren Air Force Base are long-standing anchors.

Newer names have joined them. Wyoming's business council lists Microsoft, Meta, Magpul, Searing Industries and Eagle Claw as major employers, and reports combined data center investment from Meta and Microsoft of more than $1.8 billion. Cheyenne Regional, the local hospital, reports more than 2,000 employees, and a Veterans Affairs medical center also serves the area.

Here is how those facts line up:

TopicFactSource
Population, July 1, 202566,507 (estimate)Census Bureau

Sellers who work for the base or a large employer may need to move on a short timeline. A transfer or a job change can leave a short window to sell.

How does Cheyenne's weather affect a house?

Cheyenne is cold and semiarid, with strong summer thunderstorms, and hail is the weather that does the most harm to a roof. The National Weather Service reports that Cheyenne sees more than 6 days a year with severe hail of an inch or larger nearby, with June the busiest month and July next.

Quarter-size hail is the most commonly reported size. Hail can fall anywhere from March into October, and most reports come late in the afternoon.

The city's own climate numbers are worth knowing too:

  • Average annual precipitation is about 15.9 inches, mostly from May through August.
  • Seasonal snowfall averages about 60 inches, with March and April the snowiest months.
  • Lows reach 0 degrees Fahrenheit on roughly nine mornings a year.
  • The growing season runs about 106 days.

For a seller, this means buyers and inspectors will look closely at shingles, gutters, siding and furnace age. A roof with visible hail bruising can lower an offer or stall a financed sale. A cash buyer who purchases as-is does not ask you to fix that first.

Is flood risk a concern when selling in Cheyenne?

Flood risk is a real topic in Cheyenne because of the flash flood of August 1, 1985. The National Weather Service recorded 6.06 inches of rain in about three hours, 12 deaths, 70 injuries and more than $61 million in damage.

After the flood, a FEMA report called for better stormwater and floodplain management, and the city adopted new drainage plans and retention projects in the late 1980s. Today the city's Engineering Services Department keeps flood insurance rate maps and base flood elevations. You can reach it at 2101 O'Neil Ave., Room 206, or by phone at (307) 637-6268.

If your home is near Crow Creek or Dry Creek, check the map before you list. A buyer's lender may require flood insurance, and finding that out late can cost you days.

Which Cheyenne permits and code rules matter before a sale?

The City of Cheyenne requires a permit for many repairs sellers consider, including reroofing, decks, garages, water heaters, and electrical, plumbing and HVAC work. Permit review can take up to 10 business days, and fees are based on project value.

Some smaller jobs are exempt. A detached shed under 200 square feet needs no permit, and flatwork such as a concrete patio generally does not, unless it is in the city right-of-way. Fences over 6 feet need a permit, and the city limits fences to 4 feet in front of the house.

  • Carports over 200 square feet, or attached to another structure, need a permit.
  • Zoning violations can carry fines of $100 per day.
  • Structures built in a setback may have to be removed.

Cheyenne treats short-term rentals like other residential uses, so there is no separate registration, but each rental must hold the approvals it needs. If you have an unpermitted deck, shed or carport, call the Building Department at (307) 637-6265 before a buyer finds it in an inspection.

When are Laramie County property taxes due?

Laramie County property taxes are due in two halves, with the first half payable by November 10 and the second half payable by May 10 of the following year. If you pay the whole bill by December 31, interest on the first half is waived.

Taxes not paid by the payable date become delinquent, and delinquent taxes accrue interest at 18 percent per year. If a bill is still unpaid on May 11, the treasurer certifies a delinquent list, and the county holds a lien that can lead to a tax sale. The Laramie County Treasurer is at 309 W. 20th Street, Cheyenne.

Property is assessed to the owner of record on January 1. If you bought or recorded a deed after that date, the notice may not carry your name, but you are still responsible for the tax. The assessor mails schedules no later than the fourth Monday in April, and you have 30 days from the mailing to file a written objection. Our Wyoming property tax guide covers appeals in more detail.

What happens at closing and recording in Cheyenne?

A deed for a Cheyenne sale is recorded with the Laramie County Clerk, and the clerk cannot accept it until a sworn statement of the price and terms is filed. Wyoming law, W.S. 34-1-142, makes that statement confidential, so the sale price does not become a public record.

The clerk's recording fee is $12 for the first page and $3 for each additional page, and documents with several legal descriptions carry an added $15.50 administrative fee. The office is at 309 W 20th St, Suite 1600, and takes e-recording through several vendors. Hours are Monday through Friday, 8:00 AM to 5:00 PM.

How does a cash sale work for a Cheyenne homeowner?

A cash sale means a buyer purchases your house without a lender, so the deal does not depend on an appraisal or loan approval. You tell us about the property, we review it, and you decide whether the offer works for you.

This route often suits sellers who face one of these situations:

  • An inherited house that needs probate paperwork and cleanout.
  • A hail-damaged roof or older systems that would fail a lender's inspection.
  • A military or job move with a fixed date.
  • Back taxes or a payment problem that is getting worse.

We buy as-is, with no commission and no closing costs charged to you, and you owe nothing if you decline an offer. Call or text (424) 435-2326 or use the form on this page to start.

More questions about Cheyenne, WY

How fast can I sell my house in Cheyenne?

A cash sale can close faster than a listing because it skips lender approval and appraisal. The exact timeline depends on title work, any probate, and the date you choose. Tell us your deadline and we will work around it.

Do I need to fix hail damage before selling in Cheyenne?

No, not if you sell to a cash buyer who purchases as-is. If you list on the open market, a hail-damaged roof often comes up in the inspection and can lower the offer or require repairs. Note that reroofing needs a City of Cheyenne permit.

Is my sale price public in Wyoming?

No. The sworn statement of consideration filed with the deed is confidential under W.S. 34-1-142 and is not a public record. The county uses it for statistical purposes.

When are property taxes due in Laramie County?

Half is payable by November 10 and half by May 10 of the next year. Interest on the first half is waived if you pay the full bill by December 31, and delinquent taxes accrue 18 percent interest per year.

Who do I call about a permit or a flood map in Cheyenne?

Call the Building Department at (307) 637-6265 for permits and Engineering Services at (307) 637-6268 for flood maps and base flood elevations. Planning and Development at (307) 637-6282 handles zoning, fences and setbacks.

Where is Casper and what is around it?

Casper is in east-central Wyoming on the North Platte River and is the county seat of Natrona County. The city sits at roughly 5,100 feet and covers about 27 square miles.

Interstate 25 is the main route in and out, approaching from the north and east, and US 20/26 runs near the airport on the west side. Casper-Natrona County International Airport has United Express and Delta Connection service. Several smaller communities touch the city limits, so a Casper address may sit in a different jurisdiction than you expect:

  • Mills
  • Evansville
  • Bar Nunn
  • Unincorporated areas such as Allendale, Dempsey Acres and Red Buttes

Before you list or sell, confirm whether your parcel is inside the City of Casper or in the county. That decides who issues permits and who enforces nuisance rules.

What is the history of Casper?

Casper began when the railroad reached the site in June 1888, and residents petitioned for incorporation in April 1889. The town took its name from Fort Caspar, which honored Lt. Caspar Collins, who was killed nearby in 1865.

Oil shaped the city. Casper's first refinery was built in 1895, the oil boom ran from about 1910 into the mid-1920s, and by 1922 the Midwest Refinery was described as the largest in the world by gasoline volume. The population jumped from 2,639 in 1910 to 11,447 in 1920.

Boom and bust followed. The Texaco refinery closed in 1982 and the Amoco refinery in 1991, and the population fell from 51,016 in 1980 to 46,742 in 1990.

What does the Casper economy look like today?

Casper is a regional center for banking, commerce and energy, and it also leans on healthcare, manufacturing and tourism. Oil, gas, mining and wind power are foundational sectors, according to the city's economic development partner, Advance Casper.

Casper Mountain, the Hogadon ski area and the North Platte River support outdoor tourism. The airport is Wyoming's only Foreign Trade Zone, and a Sinclair refinery operates in nearby Evansville.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported a mean hourly wage of $28.93 in the Casper metro in May 2025, compared with $33.54 nationally. Here are the largest occupation groups it listed:

Occupation groupShare of local jobsMean hourly wage
Office and administrative support10.6%$22.84
Food preparation and serving9.8%$15.21
Sales and related9.6%$23.99
Transportation and material moving9.4%$24.84
Construction and extraction8.1%$28.98

Energy and construction jobs make up a large part of local work, so a slowdown can strain an owner's budget. A missed payment can turn into a sale decision.

How does Casper's climate affect a house?

Casper has long, cold, dry winters and hot, mostly dry summers, so heating systems and roofs take the most wear. The normal January high is 35.2 degrees Fahrenheit and the normal July high is 89.0.

  • Average annual snowfall is about 71.8 inches.
  • Average annual precipitation is 12.22 inches.
  • Highs reach 90 degrees on about 38 days a year.
  • Lows drop to 0 degrees on about 15 nights a year.

Snow can be extreme. In the storm of April 3 and 4, 2023, Casper recorded 26.7 inches of snow in a day and 37.4 inches over two days, both records. After a roof collapsed at a commercial building, the Natrona County building official listed warning signs for owners to watch: creaking, visible sagging, cracked or split wood members, cracks in walls and doors that pop open.

If your roof, ceilings or walls show any of those signs, a buyer's inspector will find them. A cash buyer who purchases as-is will still look at them, but you will not have to repair them before closing.

Does Casper have flood or burn scar risk?

Parts of Casper can see flash flooding, especially downstream from the slopes of Casper Mountain. On July 29, 2013, the National Weather Service issued a flash flood warning for the east side of Casper after heavy rain fell on a recent burn scar from the Sheep Herder Hill fire.

Several homes along the Clear Fork of Muddy Creek were damaged, and flooding was reported on East Second Street between Wyoming Blvd. and Hat 6 Road. Much of that day's rainfall came in about 20 minutes.

If your home is on the east side or near a creek, check flood maps and ask your insurer about coverage before a buyer's lender does. Tell a buyer about any past water problem up front.

What permits and code rules apply to Casper sellers?

The City of Casper requires building permits for most projects, and it has adopted the 2021 International Codes, including the building, residential, fire, plumbing, mechanical and fuel gas codes. Amendments are in Title 15 of the municipal code.

Small jobs have different rules. Sheds under 120 square feet do not need a building permit, and a fence not over 6 feet high needs a fence permit but not a building permit. Platforms and walkways not more than 30 inches above grade are exempt from the building permit, while taller decks likely are not.

The Code Enforcement Division handles nuisance complaints. Typical issues include:

  • Weeds and overgrowth
  • Litter and accumulated junk
  • Junk vehicles
  • Dangerous buildings
  • Recreational vehicle parking

The city notifies the owner or tenant first and asks for a correction. If the problem is not fixed, the case may be referred to Municipal Court. Residents file complaints through the Casper 311 online form.

When are Natrona County property taxes due?

Wyoming property taxes are due in two halves, with the first half payable by November 10 and the second half payable by May 10 of the following year. Paying the full amount by December 31 avoids interest and penalty on the first half under the statute.

Taxes still unpaid on May 11 are declared delinquent, and the county treasurer then demands payment. Natrona County offers an online payment portal that asks for your bill number, tax year, last name and total tax bill. The county's main office is at 200 N Center, Casper, and the phone is 307-235-9200.

Because the tax follows the property, an unpaid bill can surface at closing. Check your balance before you sign a contract. Our Wyoming property tax guide explains the appeal process.

What should Casper sellers know about the deed and sale price?

A deed for a Casper sale must come with a sworn statement of the full price and terms, and Wyoming law keeps that statement confidential. Under W.S. 34-1-142, the county clerk cannot record the deed until the statement is filed.

The statement is not a public record, and the county may use it only for statistical sales-price ratios. Transfers such as foreclosure sales and certain gifts between family members are exempt from the price disclosure.

For recording fees and procedures, call the Natrona County main office at 307-235-9200, since the county page we reviewed does not list the clerk's fees.

How does a cash sale work for a Casper homeowner?

A cash sale means we buy your house without a lender, so the sale does not hinge on a bank appraisal or loan approval. You share a few details about the home, we review them, and you decide whether to accept.

We buy as-is, with no commission and no closing costs charged to you, and you owe nothing if you turn the offer down. This option can fit a house with an old roof, deferred repairs, a code enforcement notice, or an estate that needs to be settled. Call or text (424) 435-2326, or fill out the form on this page.

More questions about Casper, WY

Can I sell a Casper house with a code violation?

Yes. A cash buyer can purchase a house that has open nuisance or permit issues, and we buy as-is. If you list the home instead, expect buyers to ask about notices from the Code Enforcement Division and about any unpermitted work.

Do I need a permit to replace a deck or fence in Casper?

Usually yes for a fence, since a fence permit is required even when the fence is not over 6 feet high. Decks not more than 30 inches above grade are exempt from the building permit, but taller ones likely need one. Confirm with the Building / Inspection Division.

When are property taxes due in Natrona County?

Half is payable by November 10 and half by May 10 of the next year. Bills unpaid on May 11 are delinquent. You can pay through the Natrona County online portal.

Is my sale price public in Wyoming?

No. The sworn statement of price filed with the deed is confidential under W.S. 34-1-142. Certain transfers, such as foreclosure sales, are exempt from the statement.

Does heavy snow damage matter when selling in Casper?

It can. Casper averages about 71.8 inches of snow a year, and the April 2023 storm set records. Buyers' inspectors look for sagging, cracks and roof wear, and a cash buyer who purchases as-is does not require those repairs first.
